entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Livius Salinator was a Roman plebeian consul, dictator (207) and censor (204), who fought in the Second Punic War, most notably during the Battle of the Metaurus.

A member of the patrician class, Salinator rose through the ranks of Roman politics, serving as a legate under the consul Appius Claudius Pulcher (205) and later as a quaestor under the dictator Publius Cornelius Scipio (207).

His military campaigns, though ultimately unsuccessful, cemented his reputation as a skilled military commander and statesman.

Salinator's actions were influenced by the complex web of alliances and rivalries between the Roman Republic and Carthage, as well as the internal power struggles within the Roman aristocracy.

The Battle of the Metaurus was a pivotal moment in the Second Punic War, marking a significant defeat for the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Barca.

The aftermath of the Battle of the Metaurus saw a shift in the balance of power between Rome and Carthage, with Rome emerging as a dominant force in the Mediterranean.

Salinator's legacy extends beyond his own military campaigns, as he played a key role in shaping the development of Roman politics and governance.

In the words of the Roman historian Livy, 'Salinator was a man of great courage and noble character, who served his country with distinction and died in the line of duty.'
